title: Muni Network: Newsrooms unite against AI disruption
summary: Facing the threats of AI-induced disruption and declining web traffic, Southeast Asian newsrooms unite through the Muni Network for the future of news

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – As artificial intelligence continues to squeeze traffic and revenue from independent media, the question of what path newsrooms need to take to survive the disruption has been at the forefront of many conversations within the industry.

Some independent newsrooms in the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries are going a step beyond talking. From November 19 to 22, editors, technology leads, and newsroom strategists from these news groups gathered at the Rappler headquarters to confront the issue and explore approaches to addressing the AI enigma that capitalize on their collective strengths and communities.

Organized and hosted by Rappler, the event, Future of News (FON) Laboratory, aimed to build a collective approach to AI disruption, declining website traffic, and unfair policies by tech platforms, striving to secure, as its name suggests, the future of news.

“Since the launch of AI overview, we have seen a 50% to 70% drop in our organic traffic coming from the search engine,” said Wahyu Dhyatmika, CEO of Indonesia’s Tempo Digital. “We have to find other ways to ensure that we still can reach our audience, can still be impactful, and also build a new business model.”Rappler CEO Maria Ressa stressed the need for a shared solution. “It doesn’t matter if one news group is moving ahead because we cannot fight these forces alone,” she said.

Ressa emphasized the need for newsrooms to find new business models and build audiences together. “That’s the other reason I wrote The Fight Back. The fight back literally is building our communities. It is bottom up with our communities, and then we have to work with our governments,” she explained.

“The November 2026 sessions follow many preliminary meetings and one-on-one sessions where we confronted difficult questions that usually got in the way of collaboration,” said Gemma Mendoza, head of strategic programs at Rappler.

Editorial leaders and representatives from Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), Mizzima (Myanmar), Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao) pose for a group photo during…

blocks.text: Newsrooms that sent participants to the Future of News Laboratory included Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), and Mizzima (Myanmar), alongside Philippine community newsrooms Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao).

Among matters discussed in preliminary sessions was Meta’s aborted effort to implement a clause in its commercial terms, which treated presence on its platforms as permission for the tech giant to scrape publisher content and use the same as training data for its AI products.

blocks.caption: MUNI-MAXXING. Some representatives from Southeast Asian newsrooms engage in a workshop on how to set up, configure, and maximize MUNI in their workflows. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Meta’s recent decision to withdraw the planned website-crawling clause in its updated commercial terms proves that collective pushback works,” said Mendoza, who also leads Rappler’s Future of News initiative.
Representatives of participating newsrooms agreed that they cannot afford to lower their guard.
“They (platforms) steal data, they use data. And the irony is we buy data back from them,” said Redempto Anda, editor-in-chief of Palawan News.

Aryo Widhy Wicaksono from Indonesia’s Katadata also noted that because people now read news straight from social media and AI summaries instead of visiting news websites, fewer brands are buying ads from publishers.
“All the news that we produce, we took effort, we took time, we took a lot of work to do that. And then the AI just took an overview [of] it without really doing anything,” Wicaksono added.

While calling out unfair practices by AI companies, the FON participants also explored ways by which newsrooms can use AI safely to improve and enrich their daily work, as long as human editors stay in control.
At Cambodia’s Kiripost, AI is already helping small teams work faster.
“Recently, our data team, without any coding experience, started a few months ago with vibe coding,” shared Tharum Bun, its co-founder and managing editor.

blocks.caption: THOUGHTS ON AI. Cambodian media company Kiripost managing editor Tharum Bun discusses his newsroom’s unique strengths and the impact of AI in their journalism. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Small web tool apps that we have never had before, now we can build in a few months, and we can produce more visual data and stories in a very effective way,” Bun added.
For Mildred Galarpe, editor-in-chief of SunStar Cebu, AI initially felt like a “shining, shimmering tool” that tempted newsrooms to adopt it without enough caution.

blocks.caption: COLLABORATION. SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe suggests community engagement efforts that newsrooms should implement, during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Galarpe noted, however, that moving too quickly led to early mistakes, such as accidentally swapping the family names of the new and old governors in their coverage due to AI use. That experience taught them that while AI is an effective tool to fast-track work, it is not the editor.

“The human eye should always be there. Nothing should be published without your thumbprint,” Galarpe said.Rappler’s Ressa further stressed that AI cannot replace humans because its models operate on probability instead of facts, meaning what many refer to as “hallucination” is actually just the system working as designed.“You will always need a human in the loop…because news is anchored in facts, but the tech that is ruling our lives, they’re anchored in profit, so it’s corrupted the entire world,” Ressa added.

To turn their stand into action, the participating newsrooms are joining forces through the Muni Network, inspired by the MUNI tab on the Rappler app.The Muni Network will officially launch on December 10, coinciding with Human Rights Day, with plans to expand across the region soon.For Anda, this network is essential for small newsrooms like theirs.

“I look at it as a startup venture, because this is something that is pioneering. You have newsrooms gathering together and figuring out a way to go around this problem of AI using our data [and] how we deal with social media platforms inundating and taking over newsrooms,” Anda added.
By combining their audiences and reach, smaller and independent newsrooms hope to achieve greater impact together, if not match the strength of global tech giants.
“AI doesn’t know boundaries,” Wicaksono said. “If we have a collaboration, we add those small sounds or small voices [to] become one.”

blocks.caption: STATUS CHECK. Some Southeast Asian newsroom representatives put their ideas, capabilities, and ways to respond to AI threats on a whiteboard during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: The federation wants to change how newsrooms work together across Southeast Asia.
Dhyatmika added that publishers won’t stand a chance if they act individually in the era of AI. For him, newsrooms should not see each other as competitors but collaborators.
He emphasized that acting collectively would enable them to get a fairer share of the value created by their products in the digital ecosystem.

Alongside the workshop, the Future of News Laboratory participants also attended Rappler’s Social Good Summit centered on the theme “We, The Humans” — a timely reminder that humans (the journalists in this situation) must remain in control of technology and use its potential to drive meaningful action instead of being driven by it.
Before the November sessions, the group had also issued a joint statement to sound the alarm on the negative effects of AI on journalism, facts, and democracy.

Released last May for World Press Freedom Day, the joint statement highlighted issues such as algorithmic suppression of news, the economic challenges posed by Big Tech monopolies, and the rise of disinformation, which collectively threaten the survival of independent media.

Early collaborators have already launched public chat channels to strengthen local journalism and held community chats around newsroom-initiated investigations. Among those who participated were Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu. Both newsrooms have their branded chat channels embedded on their respective websites.

In September 2025, in time for World News Day, the collaboration also released an experimental video simulating Replica, an “AI-powered journalist.” The video aimed to send a dire warning about what could happen if independent newsrooms die and the only source of news would be AI, ending with a call for citizens to support real journalism. – Rappler.com
